Press Release:


Stop the slaughter
It’s called a Driven Hunt. Valuable game - including buck, baboon and warthog - will be driven down a dedicated path by farm workers. Then it’s a free-for-all as hunters atop raised scaffolding take aim at hundreds of animals herded to the slaughter. Foreign hunters are lining up to take part in the Hunt in Limpopo on Monday and the community who own the land support the hunt for the revenue it will generate. Carte Blanche investigates.
VOTE IN OUR POLL: Carte Blanche is running a poll on the subject asking ‘Should this practice be outlawed?’ To vote, visit the Carte Blanche website.


Script:


DRIVEN HUNTING

V/O: The massive outcry over the illegal killing of Cecil the lion put trophy hunters squarely in the sites of critics worldwide. But no sooner had the global roar of disapproval died down, than a new storm erupted on social media this week. It all began in the Carte Blanche offices on Tuesday. 18

Devi: Early this morning we discovered an email that had been sent to CB, and the email is rather disturbing. It talks about a planned hunt involving hundreds of animals in the Alldays area.

V/O: We received photos of wooden platforms placed in rows in the bushveld. The source claimed hundreds of animals would be slaughtered by foreign hunters on these farms in what is known as a driven hunt. We called the farm manager, Ismael Moola. 14.5

Devi: I was told about a driven hunt that is going to be taking place in Alldays this Saturday. So I just wanted to phone and ask if this is true?

Ishmael: We do have a hunt that is coming up, that I’ll agree.

V/O: And so began a convenient avoidance of the word “driven”. Driven hunting has been practiced for centuries in Europe, and usually involves beaters driving birds, deer or wild boar towards a line of hunters. It’s controversial because in the high speed chase many animals are wounded, not killed outright.
But driven hunting in Africa is virtually unheard of, which is why it’s not even mentioned in our legislation. 29

Link: Driven hunting is not illegal in SA, but it’s widely considered to be unethical and inhumane. We’ve come here to the NSPCA. They have a national responsibility to prevent cruelty against animals.

Ainsley: It’s absolutely absurd, these animals have no chance of escaping attack and also there’s no way of ensuring that these animals will actually be killed because it’s a far different cry from a hunter who sits and stalks a prey and waits and lines up and takes the perfect shot on a stationary animal.

V/O: Ainsley Hay is the Manager of their Wildlife Protection Unit. 3.5

Ainsely: These animals are going to be terrified. They’re being actively chased through the bush, they’re going to be scared, they’ve got a whole bunch of them running together which is completely unnatural. They’re moving targets. So it’s just going to be, it’s going to be horrendous!

Devi: How is the NSPCA getting involved now? What are you going to do?

Ainsley: We’re sending inspectors up to go and investigate on the scene. We need to see exactly what’s happening and then based from our investigation and our findings, we will then take whatever steps we can. But unfortunately this is legal.

V/O: And so we travelled up to Limpopo to investigate the claims. We arrived in Alldays, and followed the SPCA inspectors out to the farms. Twenty kilometers out of town we saw the first signs of the wooden platforms. But nothing could prepare us for the sheer scale of what we found. Miles and miles of wooden structures lined six firebreaks, stretching as far as the eye could see. 27.5

Isabel: Now that we’ve seen it we know it’s true. And it’s still going to happen, and we never know, it might have happened already.

V/O; Isabel Wentzel is the Senior Inspector for the Wildlife Protection Unit. 5

Devi: So what happens now? What do you do?

Isabel: Well we are actually going to go now to the farm. It is a complaint, so we are handling it as a complaint that this is about to happen, and we are worried about the animals.

V/O: But the farm manager came to us. 2

Devi: Howzit, are you Ishmael?

Ishmael: You’re blocking the road, I need to go. You’re blocking my road.

Devi: The NSPCA is here though, they want to speak to you guys. We’ve actually come with them.

Ishmael: You can speak to Simon please.

Isabel: Who is Simon?

Ishmael: Simon Mafela.

Devi: Is it a driven hunt?

Ismael: I have no comment on that.

Devi: But you are the farm manager?

Ismael: I am the farm manager who takes care of my animals, that waters them.

Devi: But it looks like a driven hunt with all the structures?

Ismael: That you will have to discuss…

Devi: Oh come on Ismael, you know if it’s a driven hunt or not a driven hunt?

Ismael: Once again, like I said I’m a farm manager.

V/O: All the wooden platforms are on Braam farm, which together with Montagu and Ammondale are owned by the Tshivula Communal Property Association. Covering 9000 hectares this successful land claim was handed over in 2009. With their strategic partner they have stocked the farms with elephant, lion, leopard and various antelope, and recently renovated Ammondale to a 5-star hunting lodge. The Secretary of the CPA is Simon Mafela. 30

Devi: I’d like to speak to you about this planned driven hunt.

Simon: I must correct you to say there is nothing like a planned driven hunt.

Devi: Oh, what is it then?

Simon: Who told you about the planned driven hunt anyway?

Devi: It doesn’t matter by who, I’m asking you is there going to be a driven hunt, yes or no?

Simon: You know what my problem is, because you are not coming to me as if you are trying to get information in an open and transparent manner.

Devi: So what are those structures for then? If it’s not for a driven hunt then what are they for?

Simon: Do you go around the farms and ask the farmers what the structures are for? No, no we are the only Black-owned farm there.

Devi: That’s not important to me. Why are you avoiding the question? So tell me what are those structures for?

Simon: Tell me who sent you?

Devi: I’m a journalist I’m doing my job.

Simon: The only thing that will be clear is whether you are a Black/White lady or White/Black lady? That will be the first thing.

Devi: What difference does my race make?

Simon: So if you come to me and tell me that you are just doing your work, you see we are also doing our work on the farm?

Devi: So what are those structures for?

Simon: Now the issue is am I compelled to tell you if I don’t know why I should tell you?

V/O: But we also showed pictures of the wooden structures to Dutch hunter John van Vessem. He knew exactly what they were for. 7.5

John: There was a picture of a driven hunt. So you see the stands where the hunters will be, and probably the drivers will come from the right side. They will get out all the game, the hunters will be in the middle and when it passes they are trying to shoot it. What was different was all the stand where the hunters will be: I thought they were pretty close together. Normally in Europe we’ve got at least 100 metres in between them, normally a little bit further. On the picture I saw they were closer together.

V/O: The day before the European hunters were scheduled to arrive at Ammondale, excited locals from Alldays told us all about the jobs they had secured for the week of the hunt. 10.5

Beater: They’re going to pay us R120 per day.

Braam: And how many days are you going to be working?

Bater: Eight days.

Braam: Starting when?

Beater: Tomorrow.

Braam: Tomorrow what time?

Beater: We’re going to start 6 to 6.

V/O: According to the Limpopo Department of Environmental Affairs, the Tshivhula CPA obtained an exemption permit a few weeks ago. This gives them freedom to hunt everything on their farms, besides threatened or protected species. We travelled to the World Heritage Site at Mapungubwe National Park to meet the Head of Department, Solly Kgopong. 22

Solly: We actually appreciate Carte Blanche bringing this information to the Department because we were not aware of this driven hunt.

Devi: How does the Department feel about driven hunting?

Solly: As I'm speaking to you now my officials are currently looking at this thing in terms of compliance. We are aware that this is not under legislation, but as the Department we need to take action where things are unethical. And I can assure you that is what the Department will pursue.

Devi: What are you going to say to your guests when the hunters arrive and you have to tell them that the NSPCA is not happy, and you have to tell them that government is also not happy in this province?

Simon: It is quite interesting because you have never seen a Black person succeeding in running a farm, and this is intriguing. And all the Whites, all the racists are mobilized around this in the name of, in the interests of I don’t know.

V/O: And then on Friday, just one day before the hunt was scheduled to begin, everything changed. 6

Link: This morning I received a call from Ismael. He invited us to a meeting at Ammondale: one condition though – no cameras, no sound recording equipment. We’re going to go in and see what we can negotiate.

V/O: Inside we were met by officials from the Department; a subdued Simon Mafela and the Dutch investor Anton de Vries, a fruit exporter from Cape Town. Finally we got some answers: a group of 13 hunters from Holland and Belgium have arrived to participate in driven hunts. Sixty beaters will drive the animals towards the hunters who will each shoot 2 or 3 animals per day. There are 600 wooden platforms on the farm. But none of this will happen until the Department gives them the go-ahead. 33

Ainsley: There’s two streams of action here: one is bombard Limpopo Nature Conservation – they are the government department that has issued the permits to happen. They have the control and the powers to stop practices like this. So, send them emails. Bombard them with emails. If they don’t answer their emails, phone them. Block their phone lines. And quite frankly if you live in Limpopo go and sit outside their offices; because you have the right to get answers to this. Second option is to go to the farm.


Devi: You can't stop this can you?

Ainsley: No.

Devi: Who can stop this?

Ainsley: Limpopo Nature Conservation and the public.






DRIVEN HUNTING PROMOS

Promo 1 (15”)

Devi: Concerned Carte Blanche viewers contacted us this week telling us about a driven hunt planned in the Alldays area of Limpopo. But it’s only when we got here that we understood exactly what it meant.

V/O: Hundreds of platforms await animals driven into the firing line.


Promo 2 (15”)

V/O: A petition to stop driven hunting in the Alldays area of Limpopo has gone viral. But how long will the animals have a reprieve?

Ainsley: Just because it’s legal doesn’t mean it’s right. We have to be there, we have to do whatever we can.

Promo 3: (10”)

V/O: “Preposterous and far-fetched” was the reaction to driven hunting in the African bushveld. But has this social media campaign managed to stop the driven hunt in Limpopo?
